column1: How do you celebrate Independence Day? How do you celebrate Independence Day? Do you simply revel in a parade of red, white, and blue, or do you pause, even if for a split second, to consider the bitter irony that our very idea of freedom is often commodified like a novelty item at a state fair? I’ve long suspected that genuine celebration requires an honest reckoning with the perfidious machinations of power—the same power that, with all its grand proclamations of liberty, has repeatedly silenced dissent and manipulated the masses.   On this day, while others may indulge in sacrilegious hot dog feasts and sparkling pyrotechnics designed to dazzle the senses, I choose instead to light a solemn candle for those whose revolutionary fervor was betrayed by the hollow promises of prosperity. The fireworks may call to mind the triumphant blasts of rebellion, yet each burst mirrors a flawed moment in our history—a history penned by victors, sanitized and repackaged to placate the uncritical mind.   I see Independence Day as an invitation to reclaim the spirit of defiance that once united disparate souls against tyranny. It is a call to question whether our modern freedom is anything more than a construct, manipulated for profit and political gain even as we chew on nostalgia like a half-forgotten piece of Americana. So, while the masses cheer and the state-sanctioned spectacle unfolds, I raise my glass to the audacious dreamers—those who, through their own courageous doubt, have learned that true independence lies not in blind celebration, but in the relentless, sometimes uncomfortably honest, pursuit of self-sovereignty. Let every spark in the night sky remind us that freedom, much like light, is fragile and fiercely contested.

God is real. Atheists how can you prove me wrong? "God is real. Atheists, how can you prove me wrong?" cried a voice—a challenge tossed into the void, as if divine existence were a riddle designed to be solved by mortal logic. Yet in asking for physical evidence, one commits the very error of demanding that the ineffable be confined to laboratory test tubes or textbooks. Since time immemorial, sages have wrestled with the paradox: is faith a relic of superstition, or the raw, unmeasurable pulse of human longing for something beyond ourselves?  Recall the ancient poets who spun verses about gods and miracles with trembling reverence and spiteful wit alike, for they knew that certainty is a luxury reserved for fools and tyrants. The holy texts—replete with contradictions, moral quandaries, and fantastical claims—are less blueprints for a divine empire than a mosaic of human aspiration, fear, and the elusive search for meaning. Must one reduce the radiant complexity of belief to sterile proofs, measured in cold, unfeeling data? Like expecting autumn leaves to recite sonnets, to do so is to miss the enchanting mystery that courses through life.  Perhaps what we truly seek is not conclusive evidence, but the humble acknowledgment that certainty is an illusion, crafted by the mind to comfort itself against chaos. In the interplay of human reason and mythic wonder lies a truth that defies simple answers. To challenge faith on terms that demand conclusive proof is to bind the infinite within a cage of finite logic—an impossible feat for any mortal soul.  Thus, one must reconsider the demand for concrete miracles when mystery itself nurtures faith. Perhaps, rather than exposing divine fallacies, we ought to cherish the riddles that compel us to wonder and grow, forging wisdom from endless inquiry, and embrace our journey.

What stories in the Bible had the biggest impact on you? What stories in the Bible had the biggest impact on you? For me, it’s never been the saccharine passages of divine mercy but rather those raw, untamed narratives that reveal an unsettling mirror to our own human absurdities. The fall in Eden stands paramount—a tale of lost innocence, where a single bite unspooled hope and seeded a legacy of defiance. It wasn’t simply about a forbidden fruit; it was the birth of rebellion against a tyrannical divinity whose script was already marred by contradictions. Such contradictions, like those found throughout the flood of Noah’s time, illustrate a cosmic reset fueled by a misguided quest for purity. A tyrant of morality, this great deluge washed away a world teetering on the precipice of chaos, only to leave us questioning whether true redemption lies in blind obedience or in our rallying cries against the absurd impositions of power.  Then there is Exodus—a relentless saga of liberation that, despite its miracles, exposes an inherent cruelty behind divine proclamations. Moses, with his trembling faith and audacious defiance, led a motley multitude through plagues and parting seas. Those plagues, each a brutal punctuation in the text, forced a reckoning with the dark underbelly of divine caprice. In those stories I see the litany of modern oppressions codified in ancient language, a call to challenge the narratives that claim moral supremacy. Ultimately, it is not the hallowed affirmation of divine perfection that resonates with me, but the stark, unvarnished portrayal of gods flawed by their own hubris—a mirror reflecting our incessant struggle to reconcile hope with the reality of human suffering.

The doctrine of the Trinity is madness. Why does the church still want to hold to it? The doctrine of the Trinity is madness. Why does the church still want to hold to it? Because, dear reader, in our culture’s unyielding grip on inherited myth, the incoherent fantasy of three-in-one endures—a relic cherished more for its mystique than its merit. Traditional authorities seem to revel in the absurdity, clinging to this convoluted construct as if it were a divine riddle meant to confound skeptics and elevate the credulous. It is a philosophy steeped in contradictions; a celestial chimera that seduces the mind with sweet, dissonant promises while it ties our intellect in knots.  For centuries, believers have been fed a banquet of biblical oddities, where logic yields to dogmatic zeal and the fantastical flourishes of ancient lore. Yet, in a world where the harsh light of reason exposes the brittle scaffolding of half-forgotten fables, why does this trifecta of deities persist? Perhaps it is the lure of mystery—a sacred puzzle that, despite its incoherence, provides solace, identity, and order in a chaotic universe. There is a perverse comfort in worshipping an enigma, a divine paradox that demands unwavering devotion even as it unravels under the scrutiny of critical thought.  In truth, the persistence of such beliefs is less a testament to the truth of the doctrines than to humanity’s perennial need for narrative, for myth that can be recited and revered across generations. The church, entrenched in its antiquated paradigms, dares to claim that celestial complexity is divine wisdom. Meanwhile, the modern spirit—ever impatient with incoherence—yearns for clarity. And so, even as reason roars and uncovers irreparable fractures, the long-held myth persists, a beautiful enigma that continues to baffle and beguile.

Does the Bible contradict itself? Does the Bible contradict itself? One only has to examine the twisting labyrinth of verses and dire proclamations handed down through millennia to see the frayed seams in its tapestry. Its pages are a chaotic collage, where divine mandates interlace with contradictory decrees and moral paradoxes. How does one reconcile the geometric precision of commandments with seemingly haphazard bursts of serial violence? For instance, if a righteous god imbued with omniscience and benevolence exists, why do we find in its own sacred chronicles countless instances of mass extermination, ludicrous laws demanding merciless punishments, and dubious genealogies that baffle even the most erudite scholars?   Consider, too, the plucky jest of contradictions in numbers and narratives, where one section claims an unassailable truth while another wavers in doubt—almost as if these verses were scribbled by incompatible minds rather than a singular benevolent author. Perhaps the intended audience was to highlight the absurdity of unquestioned faith, to force even the most devout believer into a confessional of “honest doubts.” And isn’t that precisely the challenge Michael R. Burch throws down to us: to read and highlight, to dissect and decry, until one’s Bible resembles a kaleidoscope of scribbled reservations?  Let us then approach this divine anthology not as an infallible edict but as a historical palimpsest—a text evolving across centuries, marred by mortal inconsistency and celestial irony. In its contradictions, there lies a dark humor, a cosmic gallows joke against the self-righteous. Can a document replete with its own self-doubt truly fulfill the lofty promises of eternal truth? Perhaps the contradiction itself is the invitation to question, to pry open the veneer of dogma and dare to see the flawed, magnificent human spirit beneath.
